A single line of writing, too blurred to read. Ukusik had been staring at it for a long while now, and still could not make out what any of the letters were.
On the line beneath it, only the first half of the writing remained: Ukusik, today—
Snap!
Ukusik shut the notebook she had snatched back out of the fire. The two names on its cover were still perfectly intact.
'From Antosha and Matvey, as a keepsake and a gift.'
Ukusik let out a long sigh and switched off the bedside lamp.

'No appetite?' Leto watched Ukusik drag her spoon back and forth through her bowl of nutrient porridge.
'I'm practicing my writing.'
'Since when are you this eager?'
'I have to learn how to write these letters, and then I'm going to ask the teacher in literacy class what they mean.'
Leto leaned in and looked at the marks Ukusik had traced across the surface of the porridge.
'What's this supposed to be? Some new language?'
'It is not!'

On Rhodes Island's open-air deck at dusk, Ukusik held up a sheet of paper and watched the wind crumple it into one strange shape after another. Then she let go. A while later, once the wind had dried her eyes and she was ready to leave, she found someone standing behind her.
'Ms. Raidian?'
Raidian combed Ukusik's ear feathers back into place with practiced hands. 'I found this piece of paper outside.'
It was Ukusik's literacy class test paper, and beside the perfect score were a few crooked, wandering strokes.
'Not even the literacy teacher can tell what those letters are supposed to be.' Ukusik's eyes, so recently dried, went wet again. 'Matvey said he and Antosha wrote all kinds of things down for me, and I can't read a single line of it!'
Raidian did not interrupt her.
'All the stories he never got the chance to tell me, all the adventures he and Antosha had, and the poem he wrote for my next birthday! He said he'd put it all in that notebook! So why wouldn't he give it to me sooner? Why did he let it fall into the fire? I could have kept it safe. I could have kept them safe!'
Raidian held her, easing the panic out of her. She knew what Ukusik most needed to hear at that moment.
'I'm sorry, Ukusik. I don't know those letters either.' Then she said, 'But...'

Ukusik switched the bedside lamp back on.
Ukusik opened that notebook again.
Ukusik looked once more at those ruined pages.
The strokes on the paper began to stir, swimming across the page and arranging themselves into shapes she knew, and the letters said: 'Ukusik, they tell me you came first in class today. That's really something. Much better than either of us ever managed at your age.'
Ukusik snorted with laughter.
'What's so funny? It's bedtime already, Ukusik. Don't tell me you're still holding out for a bedtime story.'
Ukusik nodded.
'Very well. Then let Antosha tell you how, the year he got into university, he managed to offend every last professor in the department on his very first day.'
Ukusik closed her eyes and watched the story unfold in front of her, and at last the drowsiness came rolling in. Just before she fell asleep, she forced her eyes open to look at the three yarn dolls she had made in her handicrafts class. Ms. Raidian, she thought, had been exactly right—
'But they can be any letters at all. They can carry any meaning you want them to carry. They belong to you, and they will always be with you.'
